subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q110.png]]
A 24-year-old man with Down syndrome presents with fever, pallor, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Review the CBC and differential shown in the image.

These findings are suggestive of:
explanation:
Common signs of ALL are hepatosplenomegaly (65%), lymphadenopathy (50%), and fever (60%). Anemia and thrombocytopenia are usually present, and the WBC count is variable. The numerous lymphoblasts are generally PAS positive.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 11; continuous question 110. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/Leukemia/3. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question: In which of the following conditions is Hgb A2 elevated?
explanation:
Hgb A2 is part of the normal complement of adult Hgb. This Hgb is elevated in β- thalassemia minor because the individual with this condition has only one normal β- gene; consequently, there is a slight elevation of Hgb A2 and Hgb F.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 11; continuous question 76. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate laboratory results with disease states/2.

subject: hematology
question: The lupus anticoagulant affects which of the following tests?
explanation:
The lupus anticoagulant interferes with phospholipid-dependent coagulation assays, such as the PT and APTT tests. The lupus anticoagulant does not inhibit clotting factor assays and does not inhibit in vivo coagulation.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.4; book question 4; continuous question 241. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Lupus / anticoagulant/2.

subject: hematology
question:
Patient History: A 12-year-old white male has visible bruising on his arms and legs, bruising after sports activities, and excessive postoperative hemorrhage after tonsillectomy 3 months ago. His family history revealed that his mother suffers from heavy menstrual bleeding, and his maternal grandfather had recurrent nosebleeds and bruising.

[[quiz-table:Laboratory Results]]
Test|Patient|Reference Range
PLT count|350 × 10³/µL|200–450 × 10³/µL
PT|11 sec|10–12 sec
APTT|70 sec|28–37 sec
TT|13 sec|10–15 sec
[[/quiz-table]]

[[quiz-table:Platelet Aggregation]]
Agonist|Result
Collagen|Normal aggregation
Epinephrine (EPI)|Normal aggregation
ADP|Normal aggregation
Ristocetin|Abnormal aggregation
[[/quiz-table]]

[[quiz-table:Confirmatory Tests]]
Test|Patient|Reference Range
VWF:RCo|25%|45%–140%
Factor VIII activity (VIII:C)|20%|50%–150%
VWF antigen|10%|45%–185%
[[/quiz-table]]

These clinical manifestations and laboratory results are consistent with which diagnosis?
explanation:
These clinical manifestations and laboratory results are consistent with von Willebrand disease. von Willebrand disease is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by abnormal PLT adhesion and aggregation. In von Willebrand disease, VWF is deficient or dysfunctional. VWF enhances the release of factor VIII from the liver, and it also forms a complex with factor VIII in the circulation. Deficient or dysfunctional VWF results in decreased factor VIII as well and, therefore, an increase in APTT values. The clinical manifestations associated with von Willebrand disease are easy bruising, epistaxis, and bleeding after surgery. The diagnostic laboratory test shows abnormal PLT aggregation to ristocetin, which is corrected by addition of normal plasma containing VWF. APTT is prolonged as a result of the deficiency of factor VIII. Factor VIII activity (VIII:C), VWF ristocetin cofactor activity (VWF:Rco), and VWF: antigenic activity (VWF:antigen) are abnormal. The PLT count and PT are normal in von Willebrand disease.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 2; continuous question 283. Topic path: Hemostasis/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/Platelet / disorders/3.

subject: hematology
question: The Coulter principle for counting of cells is based on the fact that:
option_a: Isotonic solutions conduct electricity better than cells do
option_b: Conductivity varies proportionally to the number of cells
option_c: Cells conduct electricity better than saline does
explanation:
Electronic cell (Coulter) counters use the principle of electrical impedance. Two electrodes suspended in isotonic solutions are separated by a glass tube that has a small aperture. A vacuum is applied, and as a cell passes through the aperture, it impedes the flow of current and generates a voltage pulse.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 21; continuous question 21. Topic path: Hematology/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Instrumentation/Cell counters/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which is the first stage of erythrocytic maturation in which the cytoplasm is pink because of the formation of Hgb?
explanation:
In normal erythrocytic maturation, Hgb formation in the late polychromatic normoblast stage gives the cytoplasm a prominent pink coloration. The RBC continues to produce Hgb throughout the reticulocyte stage of development.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 32; continuous question 32. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Microscopic / morphology/1.

subject: hematology
question: All of the following factors may influence the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) except:
option_a: Blood drawn into a sodium citrate tube
explanation:
EDTA and sodium citrate can be used without any effect on the ESR. Anisocytosis and poikilocytosis may impede rouleaux formation, thus causing a low ESR. Plasma proteins, especially fibrinogen and immunoglobulins, enhance rouleaux, increasing the ESR. Reference ranges must be established for tubes of different calibers.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 19; continuous question 19. Topic path: Hematology/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/ESRs/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following parameters may be similar for the anemia of inflammation and IDA?
explanation:
Thirty to fifty percent of the individuals with anemia of chronic inflammation demonstrate a microcytic hypochromic blood picture, with decrease in serum iron. Serum iron is decreased because it is unable to escape from the RE cells to be delivered to the NRBCs in bone marrow.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 12; continuous question 77. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/2 /.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q155.png]]
Review the following scatterplot, histograms, and automated values for a 21-year-old college student. WBC differential: 5 band neutrophils; 27 segmented neutrophils; 60 atypical lymphocytes; 6 monocytes; 1 eosinophil; 1 basophil What is the presumptive diagnosis?
explanation:
Lymphocytosis with numerous atypical lymphocytes is a hallmark finding consistent with the diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis. The automated results demonstrated abnormal WBC subpopulations, specifically lymphocytosis as well as monocytosis. However, on peripheral blood smear examination, 60 atypical lymphocytes and only six monocytes were noted. Atypical lymphocytes are often misclassified by automated cell counters as monocytes. Therefore, the automated analyzer differential must not be released and the manual differential count must be relied on for diagnostic interpretation.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 7; continuous question 155. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge to identify sources of error/Instrumentation/3 /. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question: All of the following are characteristics of megaloblastic anemia except:
explanation:
Megaloblastic anemias are associated with ineffective erythropoiesis and, therefore, a decrease in the reticulocyte count.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.4; book question 3; continuous question 80. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Anemia/Megaloblastic/2.

subject: hematology
question: All of the following are associated with intravascular hemolysis except:
explanation:
Methemoglobin occurs when iron is oxidized to the ferric state. Normally, iron is predominantly in the ferrous state in the Hgb that circulates. During intravascular hemolysis, the RBCs rupture, releasing Hgb directly into the bloodstream. Haptoglobin is a protein that binds to free Hgb. The increased free Hgb in intravascular hemolysis causes depletion of haptoglobin. As haptoglobin is depleted, unbound Hgb dimers appear in the plasma (hemoglobinemia) and are filtered through the kidneys and reabsorbed by the renal tubular cells. The renal tubular uptake capacity is approximately 5 g/day of filtered Hgb. Beyond this level, free Hgb appears in urine (hemoglobinuria). Hemoglobinuria is associated with hemoglobinemia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.2; book question 17; continuous question 52. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Anemia/Hemolytic/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following can shift the Hgb oxygen (O2) dissociation curve to the right?
explanation:
Increases in 2,3-DPG, acidosis, and hypoxia and rise in body temperature all shift the Hgb O2 dissociation curve to the right. In anemia, although the number of RBCs is reduced, the cells are more efficient at O2 delivery because there is an increase in RBC 2,3-DPG. This causes the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to shift to the right, allowing more O2 to be released to tissues.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 33; continuous question 33. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/O2 dissociation / curves/2.

subject: hematology
question: SITUATION: A differential shows reactive lymphocytes, and the physician suspects that a viral infection is the cause. What is the expected laboratory finding in a patient with a cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection?
explanation:
If both the heterophile antibody test and the EBV-IgM tests yield negative results in a patient with reactive lymphocytosis and a suspected viral infection, serum should be analyzed for IgM antibodies to CMV. CMV belongs to the herpes virus family and is endemic worldwide. CMV infection is the most common cause of heterophile-negative infectious mononucleosis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 10; continuous question 97. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/Differentials/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: A 50-year-old patient is suffering from pernicious anemia. Which of the following laboratory data are most likely for this patient?
explanation:
Patients with pernicious anemia demonstrate pancytopenia with low WBC, PLT, and RBC counts. Because this is a megaloblastic process and a DNA maturation defect, all cell lines are affected. In bone marrow, this results in abnormally large precursor cells, maturation asynchrony, hyperplasia of all cell lines, and a low M:E ratio.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.4; book question 6; continuous question 83. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Anemias/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is the preferred site for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy in an adult?
explanation:
The iliac crest is the most frequently used site for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy. This site is the safest and most easily accessible, with the bone being just beneath the skin, and neither blood vessels nor nerves are in the vicinity.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 3; continuous question 3. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Bone marrow/1.

subject: hematology
question: Neutrophil phagocytosis and particle ingestion are associated with an increase in O2 utilization called respiratory burst. What are the two most important products of this biochemical reaction?
explanation:
The biochemical products of the respiratory burst involved in neutrophil particle ingestion during phagocytosis are H2O2 and O2–. The activated neutrophil discharges the enzyme NADPH oxidase into the phagolysosome, where it converts O2 to O2–, which is then reduced to H2O2.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 11; continuous question 98. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/WBC kinetics/2.

subject: hematology
question: What is the typical reference range for relative lymphocyte percentage in the peripheral blood smear from a 1-year-old child?
explanation:
The mean relative lymphocyte percentage for a 1-year-old child is 61% compared with the mean lymphocyte percentage of 35% in an adult.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 5; continuous question 92. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/Differential / normal values/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: In which of the following conditions does LAP show the least activity?
explanation:
CML shows the least LAP activity, whereas the LAP score is slightly to markedly increased in each of the other states.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 14; continuous question 137. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/LAP score/1.

subject: hematology
question: When performing a factor VIII activity assay, a patient’s plasma is mixed with:
option_c: Plasma with a high concentration of factor VIII
explanation:
Coagulation factor assays are based on the ability of the patient’s plasma to correct any specific factor–deficient plasma. To measure for factor VIII activity in a patient’s plasma, diluted patient plasma is mixed with factor VIII–deficient plasma. The APTT test is performed on the mixture. Each laboratory should calculate its own normal ranges, which are based on the patient population, reagents, and instrument used. A range of 50% to 150% is considered normal.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.3; book question 12; continuous question 226. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Factor assay/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: What is the approximate incidence of antiphospholipid antibodies in the general population?
explanation:
The incidence of antiphospholipid antibodies in the general population is about 1% to 2%.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.4; book question 27; continuous question 264. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/LA/1.

subject: hematology
question: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) staining performed on a patient gives the following results: 10(0) 48(1+) 38(2+) 3(3+) 1(4+) Calculate the LAP score.
explanation:
One hundred mature neutrophils are counted and scored. The LAP score is calculated as follows: (the number of 1+ cells × 1) + (2+ cells × 2) + (3+ cells × 3) + (4+ cells × 4). That is, 48 + 76 + 9 + 4 = 137. The reference range is approximately 20 to 130.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 9; continuous question 132. Topic path: Hematology/Calculate/LAP score/2.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q165.png]]
Refer to the following scatterplot, histograms, and automated values for a 53-year-old man who had undergone preoperative laboratory testing. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation:
β-thalassemia minor can be easily detected by noting an abnormally elevated RBC count and Hct that does not correlate with the elevated RBC count, in conjunction with a decreased MCV. Although thalassemia and IDA are both microcytic, hypochromic processes, thalassemia can be differentiated from IDA because in IDA the RBC count, Hgb, and Hct values are usually decreased along with MCV. Although the RBC count is increased in PV, Hct must also be greater than 50% for a diagnosis of PV to be considered.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 17; continuous question 165. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/3. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question: The anticoagulant of choice for most routine coagulation studies is:
explanation:
The anticoagulant of choice for most coagulation procedures is sodium citrate (3.2%). Because factors V and VIII are more labile in sodium oxalate, heparin neutralizes thrombin, and EDTA inhibits thrombin’s action on fibrinogen, these anticoagulants are not used for routine coagulation studies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 3; continuous question 169. Topic path: Hemostasis/Select methods/Reagents/Specimen collection and handling/Specimen/1.

subject: hematology
question: All of the following are associated with sideroblastic anemia except:
explanation:
Sideroblastic anemias are a group of disorders characterized by hypochromic anemia, ineffective erythropoiesis, an increase in serum and tissue iron, and the presence of ringed sideroblasts in bone marrow.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 7; continuous question 72. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease / states/Anemia/Sideroblastic/2.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q152.png]]
Review the scatterplot of WBCs shown. Which section of the scatterplot denotes the number of monocytes?
explanation:
WBC identification is facilitated by analysis of the impedance, conductance, and light- scattering properties of WBCs. The scatterplot represents the relationship between volume (x-axis) and light scatter (y-axis). Monocytes account for the dots in section A, neutrophils are represented in section B, eosinophils are represented in section C, and lymphocytes are denoted in section D.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 4; continuous question 152. Topic path: Hematology/Apply basic principles to interpret results/Automated cell counting/2. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q162.png]]
Review the CBC and differential shown in the image for a 70-year-old man.

What is the most likely diagnosis on the basis of these values?
explanation:
CLL is a disease of older adults, classically associated with an elevated WBC count and relative and absolute lymphocytosis. CLL is twice as common in men, and smudge cells (WBCs with little or no surrounding cytoplasm) are usually present in the peripheral blood smear. CLL may occur with or without anemia or thrombocytopenia. The patient’s age and lack of blasts rule out ALL. Similarly, the patient’s age and lack of atypical lymphocytes make infectious mononucleosis unlikely. Myelodysplastic syndromes may involve the erythroid, granulocytic, or megakaryocytic cell lines but not the lymphoid cells.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 14; continuous question 162. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/2 /. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q154.png]]
Review the following CBC results for a 2-day-old infant. These results indicate:
explanation:
During the first week of life, an infant has an average Hct of 55 mL/dL. This value drops to a mean of 43 mL/dL by the first month of life. The mean MCV of the first week is 108 fL; after 2 months, the average MCV is 96 fL. The mean WBC count during the first week is approximately 18 × 109/L, and this drops to an average of 10.8 × 109/L after the first month. The PLT count in newborns falls within the same normal range as in adults.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 6; continuous question 154. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Normal values/2. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following anticoagulant drugs can be used in patients with HIT?
explanation:
Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor drug and used in patients with HIT who cannot tolerate heparin or LMWH therapy. Warfarin should not be used for anticoagulation in persons with HIT because it causes a fall in protein C concentration and vitamin K–dependent coagulation factors. Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.4; book question 41; continuous question 278. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Therapies/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: The following results were obtained on a patient: normal PLT count and function, normal PT, and prolonged APTT. Which of the following disorders is most consistent with these results?
explanation:
Hemophilia A is associated with deficiency of factor VIII, resulting in bleeding and abnormal APTT. The PLT number and function are normal in this disorder. Von Willebrand disease is a disorder of PLT adhesion associated with decreased VWF and factor VIII, causing an abnormal PLT function test result and abnormal APTT. Both Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard–Soulier syndrome cause abnormal PLT aggregation but do not cause abnormal APTT.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.3; book question 10; continuous question 224. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Coagulation disorders/3.

subject: hematology
question: When performing a mixing study, the patient’s APTT is corrected to 12% of normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?
option_c: The laboratory protocol should be followed for the interpretation of correction
option_d: A circulating anticoagulant can be ruled out
explanation:
Interpretation of correction studies varies among different laboratories. Some define correction when the mixing study result falls within 10% of the normal plasma; other laboratories conclude correction when the mixing result falls within 5 seconds of normal plasma, or a value within the APTT reference range. Only 50% factor activity is required for normal PT or APTT. A circulating anticoagulant typically results in failure to correct the APTT with normal plasma.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 7; continuous question 288. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Mixing studies/3 /.

subject: hematology
question: What is the basic hematological defect seen in patients with thalassemia major?
explanation:
In thalassemia major, there is little or no production of the β-chain, resulting in severely depressed or no synthesis of Hgb A. Severe anemia is seen, along with skeletal abnormalities and marked splenomegaly. The patient is usually supported with transfusion therapy.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 8; continuous question 73. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological / characteristics/Hemoglobinopathy/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which type of acute myeloid leukemia is called the true monocytic leukemia and follows an acute or subacute course characterized by monoblasts, promonocytes, and monocytes?
explanation:
Acute monocytic leukemia has an incidence of 1% to 8% of all acute leukemias. It has a distinctive clinical manifestation of monocytic involvement, resulting in skin and gum hyperplasia. The WBC count is markedly elevated, and prognosis is poor.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 5; continuous question 104. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Leukemia/2.

subject: hematology
question: The following laboratory results were obtained from a 40-year-old woman: PT = 20 sec; APTT = 50 sec; TT = 18 sec. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Fibrinogen (factor I) is a clotting protein of the common pathway and is evaluated by TT. In hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen concentration less than 100 mg/dL), PT, APTT, and TT are prolonged. In factor VII deficiency, APTT is normal; in factor VIII deficiency, PT is normal; and in factor X deficiency, TT is normal.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.3; book question 11; continuous question 225. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Factor deficiency/3.

subject: hematology
question: The autohemolysis test result is positive in all of the following conditions except:
explanation:
The autohemolysis test result is positive in G6PD and PK deficiencies and in HS but is normal in PNH because lysis in PNH requires sucrose to enhance complement binding. The addition of glucose, sucrose, or adenosine triphosphate (ATP) corrects autohemolysis of HS. Autohemolysis of PK can be corrected by ATP.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.2; book question 15; continuous question 50. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory tests/Special tests/2.

subject: hematology
question: The P2Y12 ADP receptor agonist assay may be used to monitor PLT aggregation inhibition to which of the following drugs?
explanation:
The VerifyNow P2Y12 test is used to assess a patient’s response to antiplatelet drugs, such as clopidogrel (Plavix) and prasugrel (Effient). These drugs are given orally along with aspirin for prevention of thrombosis or as alternative antiplatelet drugs for patients who cannot tolerate or are not sensitive to aspirin. Clopidogrel and prasugrel prevent PLT aggregation by irreversibly binding to P2Y12, which is a PLT membrane receptor for ADP. The VerifyNow P2Y12 test is a whole blood test and uses ADP as an aggregating agent to measure the level of PLT aggregation impaired by these medications. The baseline value for PLT aggregation is established. The percent (%) change from baseline aggregation is calculated and reported as % P2Y12 inhibition.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 21; continuous question 212. Topic path: Hemostasis/Selected methods/Reagents/Special tests/2.

subject: hematology
question: A manual WBC count is performed. Eighty WBCs are counted in the four large corner squares of a Neubauer hemacytometer. The dilution is 1:100. What is the total WBC count?
explanation:
The formula for calculating manual cell counts using a hemacytometer is: # cells counted × 10 (depth factor) × dilution factor ÷ area counted in mm2 or (80 × 10 × 100) ÷ 4 = 20,000/µL or 20.0 × 109/L

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 2; continuous question 150. Topic path: Hematology/Calculate/Cell count/2.

subject: hematology
question: The basic pathophysiological mechanisms responsible for producing signs and symptoms in leukemia include all of the following except:
option_a: Replacement of normal marrow precursors by leukemic cells causing anemia
option_b: Decrease in functional leukocytes causing infection
explanation:
A normal physiological response to anemia would be an increase in the kidney’s production of erythropoietin. The accumulation of leukemic cells in bone marrow leads to marrow failure, which manifests as anemia, thrombocytopenia, and granulocytopenia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 4; continuous question 103. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Leukemia/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following instruments can be used to evaluate PLT function?
explanation:
All of the instruments listed can be used to evaluate PLT function. PLT function testing is done either to determine the cause of bleeding in a patient with normal PLT count and normal coagulation tests or to assess the efficacy of antiplatelet drugs. PLT aggregometry is used for the diagnosis of inherited PLT disorders. A PLT aggregometer uses PLT-rich plasma to measure PLT aggregation in response to different PLT aggregating agents by measuring light transmission. A Lumi- aggregometer uses whole blood and has the ability to measure dense-granule secretion (by using a luminescent marker) in addition to PLT aggregation. The VerifyNow measures a patient’s response to multiple antiplatelet drugs, including aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors. The Platelet Function Ananlyzer-100 (PFA-100) is used as a screening tool for PLT function, and has replaced the bleeding time test. It uses citrated whole blood and two cartridges. Whole blood (800 μL) is put into each test cartridge. Vacuum is used to move the blood through a very thin glass tube that has been coated with a membrane containing collagen and either EPI or ADP. This coating activates the PLTs in the moving sample and promotes PLT adhesion and aggregation. The time it takes for the clot to form inside the glass tube and prevent further flow is measured as the closure time (CT). Initial screening is done with collagen/EPI. If CT is normal, it is unlikely that PLT dysfunction exists. The collagen/ADP membrane is used to confirm an abnormal collagen/EPI test result. If both tests show abnormal results, it is likely that the patient has a PLT dysfunction, and further testing for inherited and acquired bleeding disorders is indicated. If collagen/ADP is normal, then the abnormal collagen/EPI test result is likely caused by aspirin sensitivity.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 22; continuous question 213. Topic path: Hemostasis/Selected methods/Reagents/Special tests/2.

These clinical manifestations and laboratory results are consistent with:
explanation:
The clinical manifestations and laboratory results in this patient are consistent with TTP. The clinical manifestations of TTP include MAHA, thrombocytopenia, fever, renal failure, and neurological symptoms. The neurological symptoms in this patient are manifested by headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. Weakness and lethargy are signs and symptoms of anemia. The manual platelet count was much lower. The coagulation tests are normal in TTP. In von Willebrand disease, the platelet count is normal and the APTT is usually abnormal. subject: hematology
question: Argatroban may be used as an anticoagulant drug in patients with:
explanation:
Argatroban is a direct thrombin-inhibiting drug and may be used as an anticoagulant in patients with HIT to prevent thrombosis. Argatroban is a small synthetic molecule that binds to free and clot-bound thrombin. Argatroban affects TT, PT, APTT, and activated clotting time (ACT) tests. The APTT test is recommended for monitoring the dosage with the target therapeutic range of 1.5 to 3.0 times the mean of the laboratory reference range. In patients with lupus anticoagulant or factor deficiencies, baseline APTT is prolonged; in these conditions, Ecarin time can be used as an alternative assay.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.4; book question 35; continuous question 272. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Therapies/2.

subject: hematology
question:
Patient History: A 1-year-old infant was admitted with recurrent epistaxis for the past 5 days. Past medical history revealed easy bruising and a severe nosebleed that had occurred when he was 3 months of age, necessitating transfusion therapy. The mother had a severe nosebleed 8 years ago. The father was reported to bleed easily after lacerations. The patient was transfused with 2 units of packed RBCs on admission.

[[quiz-table:Admission Laboratory Results]]
Test|Patient|Reference Range
Hgb|4.5 g/dL|13–15 g/dL
Platelet count|249 × 10⁹/L|150–450 × 10⁹/L
PT|11.2 sec|11–13 sec
APTT|34 sec|28–37 sec
[[/quiz-table]]

[[quiz-table:Additional Laboratory Tests]]
Test|Patient|Reference Range
Factor VIII assay|70%|50%–150%
[[/quiz-table]]

[[quiz-table:Platelet Aggregation]]
Agonist|Result
ADP|Abnormal
Epinephrine (EPI)|Abnormal
Thrombin|Abnormal
Ristocetin|Normal
[[/quiz-table]]

These clinical manifestations and laboratory results are consistent with which condition?
explanation:
These clinical manifestations and laboratory results are consistent with Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Epistaxis and easy bruising are characteristics of platelet disorders. The positive family history is indicative of an inherited bleeding disorder. Laboratory tests reveal a low Hgb level caused by epistaxis. The normal platelet count rules out any quantitative platelet disorder. The platelet count is typically low in Bernard– Soulier syndrome. Normal PT and APTT, combined with a normal factor VIII assay, rule out coagulation disorders. The laboratory tests that confirm an inherited platelet disorder are PLT aggregation studies. PLT aggregation is normal to ristocetin and abnormal to ADP, EPI, and thrombin. These results are consistent with Glanzmann thrombasthenia. PLT aggregation is abnormal to ristocetin in von Willebrand disease and Bernard–Soulier syndrome.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 13; continuous question 294. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Platelet disorders/3 /.

subject: hematology
question: A correction is necessary for WBC counts when NRBCs are seen on the peripheral blood smear because:
option_a: The WBC count would be falsely lower
option_b: The RBC count is too low
option_d: NRBCs are confused with giant PLTs
explanation:
Automated hematology analyzers enumerate all nucleated cells. NRBCs are counted along with WBCs, falsely elevating the WBC count. To correct the WBC count, the number of NRBCs per 100 WBCs should be determined. Corrected WBC count = (uncorrected WBC count ÷ [NRBC’s + 100]) × 100.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 22; continuous question 22. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to take corrective action according to predetermined / criteria/Leukocytes/2.

subject: hematology
question: An APTT test is performed on a patient and the result is 50 sec (reference range 27–37 sec). The instrument flags the result because of failure of the delta check. The patient had had an APTT of 35 sec the previous day. The technologist calls the nursing unit to check whether the patient is on heparin therapy. The patient is not receiving heparin. What is the next appropriate step?
option_a: Check the patient’s family history for inherited factor VIII deficiency
option_b: Check to see if the patient has received any other anticoagulant medications
explanation:
Traditional anticoagulant drugs, such as heparin and warfarin, are well known. Newer anticoagulant drugs are available for the treatment and prevention of thrombosis. Some of these new drugs have AT or anti–factor Xa effects and, therefore, increase PT, APTT, and TT. Examples of these drugs are argatroban, which inhibits thrombin, and fondaparinux, which inhibits factor Xa.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 17; continuous question 298. Topic path: Hemostasis/Select course of action/3.

subject: hematology
question: A 30-year-old woman develops signs and symptoms of thrombosis in her left lower leg after 5 days of heparin therapy. The patient had had open-heart surgery 3 days previously and has been on heparin ever since. Which of the following would be most helpful in making the diagnosis?
explanation:
The PLT count should be checked every other day in patients receiving heparin therapy. HIT should be suspected in patients who are not responding to heparin therapy and/or are developing thrombocytopenia (50% below the baseline value) and thrombotic complications while on heparin therapy. Increase in heparin dose should be avoided in patients with the clinical symptoms of thrombosis while they are receiving heparin. Fibrinogen assay and PT are not the appropriate assays for monitoring heparin therapy, nor are they used to test for HIT.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 4; continuous question 285. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Heparin therapy/3.

subject: hematology
question: A standard blue-top tube filled appropriately (with 4.5 mL blood) was submitted to the laboratory for preoperative PT and APTT testing. The results of both tests were elevated. The patient’s PT and APTT from the previous day were within normal limits, and he was not on heparin therapy. Which is the most appropriate first step to investigate the abnormal results?
option_c: Check the sample for a clot
explanation:
A clot can form because of inadequate mixing of the sample after venipuncture, if the blood fills the evacuated tube at a slow rate, or with traumatic venipuncture. In vitro, blood clots result in consumption of the clotting factors and, therefore, prolongation of PT, APTT, and other clot-based assays. If the clotting factors have been activated but the clot formation is incomplete, it may result in shortening of PT and APTT. Checking the sample for a clot is the most reasonable step in this case.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 8; continuous question 289. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge to identify sources of errors/Specimens/3.

subject: hematology
question: Which test is used to monitor heparin therapy?
explanation:
Heparin dosage can be best monitored by the chromogenic anti–factor Xa assay. In anti–factor Xa assay, the concentration of heparin is determined by inhibition of factor Xa by AT. Anti–factor Xa assay uses a reagent with a fixed concentration of factor Xa and AT. Heparin forms a complex with AT and factor Xa reagents. Excess factor Xa combines with the chromogenic substrate to form a colored product; the color intensity is inversely proportional to the concentration of heparin. PT would be prolonged in heparin therapy, but the PT test is not sensitive enough to be used to monitor heparin therapy. Heparin inhibits thrombin and, therefore, causes prolonged TT. The TT test, however, is not used to monitor heparin therapy either.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.4; book question 12; continuous question 249. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Heparin therapy/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following Hgb configurations is characteristic of Hgb H?
explanation:
The structure of Hgb H is β4. Hgb H disease is a severe clinical expression of α- thalassemia in which only one α-gene out of four is functioning.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 34; continuous question 34. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Hemoglobin/2.

subject: hematology
question: A 60-year-old patient was admitted to a hospital for a liver biopsy. The biopsy was scheduled for 11:00 a.m. The coagulation results obtained at the time of admission revealed prolonged PT with an INR of 4.5. What is the physician’s most appropriate course of action?
option_a: Proceed with biopsy because prolonged PT is expected in liver disease
option_b: Postpone the procedure for a couple of days
option_c: Cancel the procedure and start the patient on vitamin K therapy
option_d: Put patient on vitamin K therapy and proceed with the procedure immediately
explanation:
Performing liver biopsy in a patient with a prolonged PT and a high INR could have life-threatening consequences. In this patient, the prolonged PT is likely caused by liver disease. Vitamin K is stored in the liver and is essential for activation of factors II, VII, IX, and X. Vitamin K needs bile (secreted by the liver) for its absorption. In liver disease characterized by obstruction, bile is not secreted into the gastrointestinal tract, and therefore, vitamin K is poorly absorbed. The most logical course of action is the following: Start the patient on vitamin K therapy, repeat the PT test 4 days after starting vitamin K administration, and cancel the biopsy until the patient’s PT returns to normal.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 15; continuous question 296. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/INR/3 /.

subject: hematology
question:
A 25-year-old woman has menorrhagia after delivery of her second son. The patient has no previous bleeding history.

[[quiz-table:Initial Laboratory Findings]]
Test|Result
PLT count|Normal
PT|Normal
APTT|Prolonged
[[/quiz-table]]

[[quiz-table:Mixing Study]]
Condition|APTT result
Immediate testing after mixing patient plasma with normal plasma|Corrected
After 2-hour incubation at 37°C|Prolonged
[[/quiz-table]]

What is the most probable cause of these laboratory results?
explanation:
Factor VIII inhibitor is found in 20% to 25% of patients with hemophilia receiving replacement therapy. It may also develop in patients with immunologic problems, women after childbirth, and patients with lymphoproliferative and plasma cell disorders, or it may develop in response to medications. Factor VIII inhibitor is an IgG with an inhibitory effect that is time and temperature dependent. The presence of factor VIII inhibitor causes elevated APTT in the face of a normal PT. Mixing studies in factors VIII and IX deficiencies will correct the prolonged APTT both at the immediate mixing stage and after incubation for 2 hours. APTT would not be corrected by mixing studies in the presence of factor VIII inhibitor. In addition, factor VIII inhibitor is associated with bleeding. Lupus anticoagulant is associated with thrombosis and not bleeding unless it coexists with thrombocytopenia, which is not the case in this patient.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 5; continuous question 286. Topic path: Hemostasis/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/Mixing studies/3.

subject: hematology
question: In myelofibrosis, the characteristic abnormal RBC morphology is that of:
explanation:
The marked amount of fibrosis, both medullary and extramedullary, accounts for the irreversible change in RBC morphology to a teardrop shape. The RBCs are “teared” as they attempt to pass through the fibrotic tissue.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 4; continuous question 127. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/RBC microscopic morphology/1.

subject: hematology
question:
A 45-year-old woman visited her doctor complaining of easy bruising and menorrhagia occurring for the past few weeks. The patient had no history of excessive bleeding during childbirth several years earlier or during a tonsillectomy in childhood. Her family history was unremarkable.

[[quiz-table:Laboratory Tests]]
Test|Patient|Reference Range
PT|45 sec|11–13 sec
APTT|125 sec|28–37 sec
TT|14 sec|10–15 sec
[[/quiz-table]]

[[quiz-table:Mixing Studies and Additional Findings]]
Test or finding|Result
PT after mixing patient plasma with normal plasma|40 sec
APTT after mixing patient plasma with normal plasma|90 sec
Platelet count and morphology|Normal
Liver function tests|Normal
[[/quiz-table]]

These clinical manifestations and laboratory results are consistent with:
explanation:
The absence of a positive family history in this patient indicates acquired coagulopathy. Because both the PT and APTT test results are abnormal, the clotting factor involved is most probably in the common pathway. The lack of correction by mixing studies suggests the presence of an inhibitor. Factor V antibodies are the most common antibodies among the clotting factors of the common pathway (I, II, V, and X). Factor V antibodies are reported to be associated with surgery; some antibiotics, such as streptomycin; exposure to blood products or the bovine form of “fibrin glue.” Patients with antibodies to factor V may require long-term therapy with immunosuppressive drugs. Acute bleeding episodes may be treated by platelet transfusions. The PT test is normal in patients with factor VIII deficiency and factor VIII inhibitor. Lupus anticoagulant is not present with bleeding unless associated with coexisting thrombocytopenia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.5; book question 20; continuous question 301. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Inhibitors/3 /.

subject: hematology
question: What is the normal WBC differential lymphocyte percentage (range) in the adult population?
explanation:
The normal adult percentage of lymphocytes in a WBC differential is between 20% and 44%, although normal ranges vary by institution, patient population, and testing methodology. This range is higher in the pediatric population.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 29; continuous question 29. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate basic laboratory values/Differentials/1 /.

subject: hematology
question: All of the following are major criteria for the 2008 WHO diagnostic criteria for ET except:
option_b: Megakaryocyte proliferation with large and mature morphology and no or little granulocyte or erythroid proliferation
option_c: Demonstration of JAK2(V617F) or other clonal marker
explanation:
In the revised 2016 WHO classification, diagnosis of ET requires meeting four major WHO diagnostic criteria, which include: PLT count 450 × 109/L or greater; bone marrow proliferation of megakaryocyte lineage with large and mature megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei and no or little granulocyte or erythroid proliferation; not meeting WHO criteria for CML, PV, PMF, MDS, or other myeloid neoplasm; and demonstration of JAK2(V617F), CALR, or MPL mutation or other clonal marker. Diagnosis can also be made with the first three major criteria and one minor criterion, either evidence of clonality or absence of reactive thrombocytosis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 25; continuous question 148. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of special procedures/Myeloproliferative / diseases/Classifications/3 /.

subject: hematology
question: Cells that exhibit positive staining with acid phosphatase and are not inhibited by tartaric acid are characteristically seen in:
explanation:
A variable number of malignant cells in HCL will stain positive with tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP+). Although this cytochemical reaction is fairly specific for HCL, TRAP activity has occasionally been reported in B-cell leukemia and, rarely, T- cell leukemia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 23; continuous question 146. Topic path: Hematology/Apply principles of special procedures/Cytochemical stains/2.

subject: hematology
question: If a patient has a reticulocyte count of 7% and Hct of 20%, what is the corrected reticulocyte count?
explanation:
In anemic states, the reticulocyte percentage is not a true measure of reticulocyte production. The following formula must be applied to calculate the corrected (for anemia) reticulocyte count. Corrected reticulocyte count = reticulocytes (%) × (Hct ÷ 45) where 45 is the average normal Hct. In this case, 7 × (20 ÷ 45) = 3.1.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 12; continuous question 12. Topic path: Hematology/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Calculate/Reticulocytes/2.

subject: hematology
question: Storage iron is usually best determined by:
explanation:
Ferritin enters serum from all ferritin-producing tissues and, therefore, is considered a good indicator of body storage iron. Because iron stores must be depleted before anemia develops, low serum ferritin levels precede the fall in serum iron associated with IDA.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 6; continuous question 71. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of basic laboratory procedures/Iron/1 /.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is the primary Hgb in patients with thalassemia major?
explanation:
Patients with thalassemia major are unable to synthesize the β-chain; hence, little or no Hgb A is produced. However, γ-chains continue to be synthesized and lead to variable elevations of Hgb F in these patients.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 9; continuous question 74. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory diseases/Hemoglobin/Hemoglobinopathy/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which type of anemia is usually present in a patient with acute leukemia?
explanation:
Acute leukemia is usually associated with a normocytic normochromic anemia. Anemia in acute leukemia is usually present from the onset and may be severe; however, there is no inherent nutritional deficiency leading to a microcytic, hypochromic, or megaloblastic process.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 2; continuous question 101. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/RBC microscopic morphology/Anemia/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following characterizes vitamin K?
option_a: It is required for biological activity of fibrinolysis
option_b: Its activity is enhanced by heparin therapy
option_c: It is required for carboxylation of glutamate residues of some coagulation factors
option_d: It is made by endothelial cells
explanation:
Vitamin K is necessary for activation of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, and X). This activation is accomplished by carboxylation of glutamic acid residues of the inactive clotting factors. The activity of vitamin K is not enhanced by heparin therapy. Vitamin K is present in a variety of foods and is also the only vitamin made by the organisms living in the intestine.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 10; continuous question 176. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Vitamin K/2.

subject: hematology
question: In ET, the PLTs are:
option_a: Increased in number and functionally abnormal
option_b: Normal in number and functionally abnormal
option_d: Decreased in number and functionally abnormal
explanation:
In ET, the PLT count is extremely elevated. These PLTs are abnormal in function, leading to both bleeding and thrombotic diathesis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 2; continuous question 125. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease / states/CBCs/Platelets/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which inclusions may be seen in leukocytes?
explanation:
Döhle bodies are RNA-rich areas within polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) that are oval and light blue. Although often associated with infectious states, they are seen in a wide range of conditions and toxic reactions, including hemolytic and pernicious anemias, chronic granulocytic leukemia, and therapy with antineoplastic drugs. The other inclusions are associated with erythrocytes.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 3; continuous question 90. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental characteristics/WBC inclusions/1.

subject: hematology
question: In which age group does ALL occur with the highest frequency?
explanation:
ALL usually affects children from ages 1 to 15 years and is the most common type of acute leukemia in this age group. In addition, ALL constitutes the single most prevalent malignancy in pediatric patients.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 6; continuous question 105. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Leukemia/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which fragments of fibrin clot degradation are measured by the D-dimer test?
explanation:
D-dimer is a specific product resulting from digestion of cross-linked fibrin only. It consists of two D domains called D-D fragment and is a marker for thrombosis and fibrinolysis. In the D-dimer test, monoclonal antibody is directed against D-dimer antigen by using a variety of automated instruments. The D-dimer test is used to diagnose acute and chronic disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and to rule out thromboembolic disorders. Fragments X, Y, D, and E are produced by the action of plasmin on fibrinogen and fibrin. Polypeptide A and B are produced by the proteolytic action of thrombin on fibrinogen to form a fibrin clot.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 11; continuous question 177. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/D-dimer/2.

subject: hematology
question: Variation in red blood cell (RBC) size observed on the peripheral blood smear is described as:
explanation:
A mature erythrocyte is approximately 7 to 8 μm in diameter. Variation in normal size is denoted by the term anisocytosis. Hypochromia is a term that indicates increased central pallor in erythrocytes, and poikilocytosis denotes variation in RBC shape.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 2; continuous question 2. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Microscopic / morphology/RBCs/1.

subject: hematology
question: Lumi-aggregation measures:
option_b: PLT aggregation and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) release
explanation:
Lumi-aggregation measures PLT aggregation and ATP release. It is performed on whole blood diluted with saline. PLT aggregation is measured by impedance, whereas ATP release is measured by addition of luciferin to a blood sample. There is no ATP release in storage pool deficiencies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 15; continuous question 206. Topic path: Hemostasis/Select methods/Reagents/Specimen collection and handling/Aggregometry/1.

subject: hematology
question: Storage pool deficiencies are defects of:
explanation:
Storage pool deficiencies are defects of PLT granules. Most commonly, a decrease in PLT-dense granules is present with decreased release of ADP, ATP, calcium, and serotonin from PLT-dense granules.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 14; continuous question 205. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Platelet disorders/1.

subject: hematology
question: Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a malignancy of the:
explanation:
Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a malignancy of lymphoplasmacytoid cells, which manufacture IgM. Although the cells secrete immunoglobulin, they are not fully differentiated into plasma cells and lack the characteristic perinuclear halo, deep basophilia, and eccentric nucleus characteristic of classic plasma cells.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 22; continuous question 145. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Immunologic / manifestation of disease/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is a characteristic of Auer rods?
option_a: They are composed of azurophilic granules
option_b: They stain positive on periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining
option_c: They are predominantly seen in chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)
explanation:
Auer rods are a linear projection of primary azurophilic granules and are present in the cytoplasm of myeloblasts and monoblasts in patients with acute leukemia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 9; continuous question 108. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Leukocytes/Auer / rods/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which reagents are used in the PT test?
explanation:
Thromboplastin and calcium (combined into a single reagent) replace tissue thromboplastin and calcium necessary, in vivo, to activate factor VII to factor VIIa. This ultimately generates thrombin from prothrombin via the coagulation cascade.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 6; continuous question 172. Topic path: Hemostasis/Select methods/Reagents/Coagulation tests/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which test would be abnormal in a patient with factor X deficiency?
explanation:
Factor X is involved in the common pathway of the coagulation cascade; therefore, its deficiency prolongs both PT and APTT. Activated factor X along with activated factor V in the presence of calcium and platelet factor 3 (PF3) converts prothrombin (factor II) to the active enzyme thrombin (factor IIa).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 7; continuous question 173. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Coagulation tests/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: Which clotting factor is not measured by the PT and APTT tests?
explanation:
Factor XIII is not measured by PT or APTT. Factor XIII (fibrin stabilizing factor) is a transamidase. It creates covalent bonds between fibrin monomers, which are formed during the coagulation process, to produce a stable fibrin clot. In the absence of factor XIII, the hydrogen bonded fibrin polymers are unstable and, therefore, soluble in 5M urea or in 1% monochloroacetic acid.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 8; continuous question 174. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Coagulation tests/1.

subject: hematology
question: Thrombocytopenia may be associated with:
option_d: Increased proliferation of pluripotent stem cells
explanation:
Hypersplenism is associated with thrombocytopenia. In this condition, up to 90% of PLTs can be sequestered in the spleen, causing decreases in circulatory PLTs. Splenectomy, acute blood loss, and increased proliferation of pluripotent stem cells are associated with thrombocytosis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 2; continuous question 193. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Platelets/2.

subject: hematology
question: Auer rods may be seen in all of the following except:
explanation:
Auer rods are not seen characteristically in lymphoblasts. They may be seen in myeloblasts, promyelocytes, and monoblasts.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 1; continuous question 100. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Acute leukemia/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the morphological findings are characteristic of reactive lymphocytes?
explanation:
Both reactive lymphocytes and blasts may have basophilic cytoplasm, a high N:C ratio, and the presence of prominent nucleoli. Blasts, however, have an extremely fine nuclear chromatin staining pattern as viewed on a Wright– and Giemsa–stained smear.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 12; continuous question 99. Topic path: Hematology/Recognize morphological changes associated with diseases/WBC morphology/2 /.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q163.png]]
Refer to the following scatterplot, histograms, and automated values for a 28-year-old woman who had undergone preoperative laboratory testing. A manual WBC differential was requested by her physician. The WBC differential was not significantly different from the automated five-part differential; however, the medical laboratory scientist noted 3+ elliptocytes/ovalocytes while reviewing the RBC morphology. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation:
The finding of ovalocytes as the predominant RBC morphology in peripheral blood is consistent with the diagnosis of HE, or ovalocytosis. This disorder is relatively common and can range in severity from an asymptomatic carrier state to homozygous HE with severe hemolysis. The most common clinical subtype is associated with no or minimal hemolysis. Therefore, HE is usually associated with a normal RBC histogram and cell indices and will go unnoticed without microscopic evaluation of the peripheral blood smear.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 15; continuous question 163. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/2. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question: IDA may be distinguished from anemia of chronic infection by:
explanation:
In IDA, serum iron and ferritin levels are decreased, and TIBC and RBC protoporphyrin are increased. In chronic disease, serum iron and TIBC are both decreased because the iron is trapped in reticuloendothelial (RE) cells and is unavailable to RBCs for Hgb production.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.3; book question 3; continuous question 68. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/Anemia/3.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is most true of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
option_a: It is a rare acquired stem cell disorder that results in hemolysis
option_b: It is inherited as a sex-linked trait
option_c: It is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait
option_d: It is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait
explanation:
PNH is a rare acquired stem cell disorder that results in abnormalities of the RBC membrane. This causes the RBCs to become highly sensitive to complement-mediated hemolysis. Because this is a stem cell disorder, abnormalities are seen in leukocytes and PLTs, as well as in RBCs. PNH is characterized by recurrent, episodic intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and venous thrombosis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.2; book question 13; continuous question 48. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/PNH/1 /.

subject: hematology
question: A patient has 80 NRBCs per 100 leukocytes. In addition to increased polychromasia on the peripheral blood smear, what other finding may be present on the CBC?
explanation:
The patient will have increased MCV. One of the causes of a macrocytic anemia that is not megaloblastic is increased reticulocyte count, here noted as increased polychromasia. Reticulocytes are polychromatic macrocytes; therefore, MCV is slightly increased.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.4; book question 10; continuous question 87. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Megaloblastic anemia/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: A manual RBC count is performed on pleural fluid. The RBC count in the large center square of the Neubauer hemacytometer is 125, and the dilution is 1:200. What is the total RBC count?
explanation:
Regardless of the cell or fluid type, the formula for calculating manual cell counts using a hemacytometer is: # cells counted × 10 (depth factor) × dilution factor ÷ area counted in mm2 or (125 × 10 × 200) ÷ 1 = 250,000/µL or 250.0 × 109/L

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 3; continuous question 151. Topic path: Hematology/Calculate/Cell count/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is characterized by:
explanation:
TTP is a quantitative PLT disorder associated with increased intravascular PLT activation and aggregation resulting in thrombocytopenia. PT and APTT results are normal in TTP.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 1; continuous question 192. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Platelets/2.

subject: hematology
question: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is a disorder of:
explanation:
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu syndrome) is a connective tissue disorder associated with telangiectases (dilated capillaries) of the mucous membranes and skin. Lesions may develop on the tongue, lips, palate, face, hands, and nasal mucosa and throughout the gastrointestinal tract. This disorder is an autosomal dominant condition that usually manifests in adolescence or early adulthood.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.2; book question 18; continuous question 209. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: “Bite cells” are usually seen in patients with:
explanation:
In patients with G6PD deficiency, the RBCs are unable to reduce nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP); consequently, Hgb is denatured, and Heinz bodies are formed. “Bite cells” appear in the peripheral circulation as a result of splenic pitting of Heinz bodies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.2; book question 19; continuous question 54. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/RBC microscopic morphology/1 /.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following organs is responsible for the “pitting process” in RBCs?
explanation:
The spleen is the supreme filter of the body, pitting imperfections from the erythrocyte without destroying the integrity of the membrane.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.2; book question 2; continuous question 37. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Physiology/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which antibiotic(s) is (are) most often implicated in the development of aplastic anemia?
explanation:
Chloramphenicol is the drug most often implicated in acquired aplastic anemia. About half the cases occur within 30 days after therapy, and about half are reversible. Penicillin, tetracycline, and sulfonamides have been implicated in a small number of cases.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.2; book question 24; continuous question 59. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Aplastic anemia/1.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following are most characteristic of the RBC indices associated with megaloblastic anemias?
explanation:
The RBC indices in a patient with megaloblastic anemia are macrocytic and normochromic. The macrocytosis is prominent, with MCV ranging from 100 to 130 fL.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.4; book question 9; continuous question 86. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Megaloblastic anemia/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following clotting factors are activated by thrombin that is generated by tissue pathway (TF-VIIa)?
explanation:
Factors V and VIII are activated by the thrombin that is generated by the action of TF-VIIa on factor X to form factor Xa. Factor Xa forms a complex with factor Va on the PLT surfaces. Factor Xa–Va complex in the presence of phospholipid and Ca2+ transform more prothrombin to thrombin.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 23; continuous question 189. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Thrombin/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is a characteristic of classic hemophilia A?
explanation:
Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is characterized by mild to severe bleeding episodes, depending on the concentration of factor VIII:C. Hemophilia A is inherited as a sex-linked disease. PLT aggregation and PT are both normal in hemophilia A.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.3; book question 6; continuous question 220. Topic path: Hemostasis/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Hemostasis/Hemophilia/2 /.

subject: hematology
question: Which protein is the primary inhibitor of the fibrinolytic system?
explanation:
α2-Antiplasmin is the main inhibitor of plasmin. It inhibits plasmin by forming a 1:1 stoichiometric complex with any free plasmin in plasma and, thus, prevents binding of plasmin to fibrin and fibrinogen.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 16; continuous question 182. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Plasmin/1.

subject: hematology
question: A Miller disk is an ocular device used to facilitate counting of:
explanation:
The manual reticulocyte count involves the counting of 1,000 RBCs. The Miller disk is a reticle (grid) that is placed in the eyepiece of the microscope and divides the field into two squares, one being nine times larger in size than the other. Reticulocytes are enumerated in both the squares. Mature RBCs are counted in the smaller one.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.1; book question 17; continuous question 17. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Manual counts/1 /.

subject: hematology
question: What would be the most likely classification by the WHO for AML M7 by the FAB classification?
option_a: Acute myeloid leukemias with recurrent genetic abnormalities
option_b: Acute myeloid leukemia with multilineage dysplasia
option_c: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia classified under AML (not otherwise categorized)
explanation:
Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, which is equivalent to FAB M7, is a relatively uncommon form of leukemia characterized by neoplastic proliferation of megakaryoblasts and atypical megakaryocytes. Recognition of this entity was aided by the use of platelet peroxidase (PPO) ultrastructural studies. PPO is distinct from myeloperoxidase and is specific for the megakaryocytic cell line. Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is defined as an acute leukemia in which 50% or greater of the blasts are of megakaryocytic lineage. In the WHO 2016 revision, it is classified under “AML (not otherwise categorized).”

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.6; book question 24; continuous question 123. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of special procedures/Leukemias/Classifications/3 /.

subject: hematology
question: Qualitative and quantitative neutrophil changes noted in response to infection include all of the following except:
explanation:
Neutrophil changes associated with infection may include neutrophilia, shift to the left, toxic granulation, Döhle bodies, and vacuolization. Pelgeroid hyposegmentation is noted in neutrophils from individuals with congenital Pelger–Huët anomaly and those with an acquired anomaly induced by drug ingestion or secondary to certain conditions, such as leukemia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 6; continuous question 93. Topic path: Hematology/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/WBC microscopic / morphology/2.

subject: hematology
question: In a patient with HIV infection, one should expect to see:
option_a: Shift to the left in WBCs
explanation:
HIV infection brings about several hematological abnormalities seen on peripheral blood smear examination; most patients demonstrate reactive lymphocytes and have granulocytopenia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.5; book question 2; continuous question 89. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease / states/HIV/Microscopic morphology/1.

subject: hematology
question: A protein that plays a role in both coagulation and PLT aggregation is:
explanation:
Factor I (fibrinogen), along with the glycoprotein IIb–IIIa complex, is necessary for PLT aggregation. Factor I is also a substrate in the common pathway of coagulation. Thrombin acts on fibrinogen to form fibrin clots.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 2 Hemostasis; section 2.1; book question 18; continuous question 184. Topic path: Hemostasis/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Clotting factors/2.

subject: hematology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch1_hematology/harr_ch1_q156.png]]
Review the following scatterplot, histograms, and automated values for a 61-year-old woman. WBC differential: 14 band neutrophils; 50 segmented neutrophils; 7 lymphocytes; 4 monocytes; 10 metamyelocytes; 8 myelocytes; 1 promyelocyte; 3 eosinophils; 3 basophils; 2 NRBCs/100 WBCs What is the presumptive diagnosis?
explanation:
The “+++++” on the printout indicates that the WBC count exceeds the upper linearity of the analyzer (greater than 99.9 × 109/L). This markedly elevated WBC count, combined with the spectrum of immature granulocytic cells seen on peripheral blood smear examination, indicates the diagnosis of CML.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.8; book question 8; continuous question 156. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease / states/Instrumentation/3. Image/result/table attachment included.

subject: hematology
question: CML is distinguished from leukemoid reaction by which of the following?
option_a: CML: low LAP; leukemoid: high LAP
option_b: CML: high LAP; leukemoid: low LAP
option_c: CML: high WBC; leukemoid: normal WBC
option_d: CML: high WBC; leukemoid: higher WBC
explanation:
CML causes a low LAP score, whereas an elevated or normal score occurs in a leukemoid reaction. CML cannot be distinguished by WBC count because both CML and leukemoid reaction have a high count.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 10; continuous question 133. Topic path: Hematology/Evaluate laboratory and clinical data to specify additional tests/Leukemias/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is often associated with CML but not with AML?
explanation:
Splenomegaly is seen in greater than 90% of patients with CML, but it is not a characteristic finding in AML. Infections, hemorrhage, and elevated WBC counts may be seen in both CML and AML.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 1 Hematology; section 1.7; book question 16; continuous question 139. Topic path: Hematology/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/CML/Characteristics/2.

subject: hematology
question: Which of the following is (are) commonly found in CML?
explanation:
CML is marked by an elevated WBC count demonstrating various stages of maturation, hypermetabolism, and minimal LAP staining. An increase in basophils and eosinophils is a common finding. Pseudo–Pelger–Huët cells and thrombocytosis may be present. Bone marrow is hypercellular, with a high M:E ratio (e.g., 10:1).
